**(B)** energy

The first law of thermodynamics states that the heat \(Q\) supplied to a system is used partly in increasing the internal energy of the system and partly by the system in doing work on its surroundings:

\(Q = \Delta U + W\), i.e. \(\Delta U = Q - W\)

Here \(\Delta U\) is the change in the internal energy of the system and \(W\) is the work done by the system. Every term in this equation is an energy, measured in joule.

The law therefore says that the energy that enters a system as heat and the energy that leaves it as work are accounted for exactly by the change in its internal energy — none of it is created and none of it is destroyed. The first law is thus nothing but the law of conservation of energy applied to a thermodynamic system, with heat recognised as a form of energy.

\(\therefore\) the first law of thermodynamics is concerned with the conservation of energy. Momentum, temperature and mass do not appear anywhere in the statement of the law.

**(A)** Zeroth law of thermodynamics

The statement refers to the **zeroth law of thermodynamics**.

**The law.** If two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third system, they are also in thermal equilibrium with each other.

**What thermal equilibrium means.** Two systems in thermal contact are said to be in thermal equilibrium if they do not transfer heat between each other, that is, if they are at the same temperature.

**Explanation.** Let \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) be three systems. If \(A\) and \(C\) are in thermal equilibrium, and \(A\) and \(B\) are in thermal equilibrium, then by the zeroth law \(B\) and \(C\) must also be in thermal equilibrium. Hence \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) are all at the same temperature.

**Importance of the law.** It shows that temperature is a measurable property common to all systems in thermal equilibrium, and so it makes the thermometer possible: when a thermometer is left in contact with an object until the two are in thermal equilibrium, the thermometer reads the temperature of the object, and the temperatures of different objects can then be compared using the same thermometer.

It is called the zeroth law because it was formulated after the first and the second laws of thermodynamics, even though it is logically the first of them.

A **thermodynamic system** is a collection or a group of objects that can form a unit and that may have the ability to exchange energy with its surroundings.

Anything that is not a part of the system is its surroundings or environment, and the system is separated from its surroundings by its boundary. For example, water kept in a vessel is the system, the vessel is its boundary, and the atmosphere around it is its surroundings.

**Types of thermodynamic systems.** Depending on what is allowed to cross the boundary, a system is classified as:

1. **Open system** — it freely allows the exchange of both energy and matter with its environment. Water boiling in an open kettle is an open system: heat escapes into the air and so does steam.
2. **Closed system** — it allows the exchange of energy but not of matter. Water boiling in a closed boiler is a closed system: heat is transferred to and from the water, but steam cannot escape while the valve is shut.
3. **Isolated system** — it is completely sealed off from its environment, so neither matter nor energy can be exchanged. A thermos flask is a familiar example.

In thermodynamics, everything that is **not** a part of the system under study is called its **surroundings** (also called its environment).

A thermodynamic system is a group of objects treated as one unit, which may be able to exchange energy with whatever lies outside it. The imaginary or real surface that separates the system from the rest of the universe is the **boundary** of the system, and everything beyond that boundary is the surroundings.

For example, if water kept in a vessel is taken as the system, then the vessel is its boundary and the atmosphere around it is its surroundings.

The exchange of heat and of work between a system and its surroundings is what the whole of thermodynamics deals with: heat flows between the two whenever their temperatures differ, and work is done whenever the system pushes against its surroundings or is pushed by them.

**Thermodynamic process.** The state of a thermodynamic system is described by its state variables — the pressure \(p\), the volume \(V\) and the temperature \(T\). A process by which two or more of these variables are changed, so that the system passes from one thermodynamic state to another, is called a **thermodynamic process** or a thermodynamic change.

In practice one of the state variables is usually held fixed while the other two are varied, and this is how thermodynamic processes are classified. Two such types are:

1. **Isothermal process** — a process in which the change in pressure and volume takes place at **constant temperature**, so \(\Delta T = 0\). It is possible when the system is in good thermal contact with its surroundings and the change is carried out extremely slowly. For an ideal gas the equation of state is then \(pV = \) constant. Melting of ice is an example.

2. **Adiabatic process** — a process in which **no heat is exchanged** between the system and its surroundings, so \(Q = 0\). It is possible when the system is thermally insulated, or when the change is so quick that there is no time for heat to flow. For an ideal gas the equation of state is then \(pV^{\gamma} = \) constant. The sudden bursting of an inflated balloon is an example.

(Isobaric — constant pressure — and isochoric — constant volume — processes are the other two types.)

A system is in thermodynamic equilibrium only when it is simultaneously in mechanical, chemical and thermal equilibrium. Two of these are asked for here.

**Mechanical equilibrium.** A system is said to be in mechanical equilibrium when there are no unbalanced forces within the system, and none between the system and its surroundings. Equivalently, a system is in mechanical equilibrium when the pressure throughout the system, and between the system and its surroundings, is the same and does not change with time. If any unbalanced force does exist inside the system, it gets neutralised in the course of time and the system then reaches mechanical equilibrium.

**Thermal equilibrium.** Two systems in thermal contact with each other are said to be in thermal equilibrium if they do not transfer heat between each other, that is, if they are at the same temperature. A system is in thermal equilibrium when the temperature is the same throughout the system, and the same as that of its surroundings, and does not change with time.

An **isothermal process** is a process in which the change in the pressure and the volume of a system takes place at a **constant temperature**. For such a change \(\Delta T = 0\), so it is a constant-temperature process.

**Conditions.** An isothermal change is possible only when the system is in good thermal contact with its surroundings, and the transfer of heat to or from the system is extremely slow, so that thermal equilibrium is maintained throughout the change.

**Equation of state.** Since the temperature is constant, Boyle's law applies to a fixed mass of an ideal gas:

\(pV = \) constant, so \(p_{i}V_{i} = p_{f}V_{f}\)

The \(p\)-\(V\) curve of such a change is called an isotherm.

**Heat and work.** The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on its temperature, so in an isothermal process \(\Delta U = 0\). The first law of thermodynamics \(\Delta U = Q - W\) then gives \(Q = W\): the whole of the heat supplied to the gas is converted into the work done by it. Neither \(Q\) nor \(W\) is zero in an isothermal process.

Melting of ice and boiling of water take place at constant temperature and are therefore isothermal processes.

**(D)** the volume increases

**Data:** the process is isothermal; the pressure decreases by \(10\%\), so \(p_{f} = 0.9\,p_{i}\).

**Relation.** For a fixed mass of an ideal gas at constant temperature, Boyle's law gives \(pV = \) constant, i.e.

\(p_{i}V_{i} = p_{f}V_{f}\)

**Final volume.**

\(V_{f} = \dfrac{p_{i}V_{i}}{p_{f}} = \dfrac{p_{i}V_{i}}{0.9\,p_{i}} = \dfrac{V_{i}}{0.9} = 1.111\,V_{i}\)

**Percentage change in volume.**

\(\dfrac{V_{f} - V_{i}}{V_{i}} \times 100 = (1.111 - 1) \times 100 = 11.1\%\)

**Check.** \(p_{f}V_{f} = (0.9\,p_{i})(1.111\,V_{i}) = 1.000\,p_{i}V_{i}\), so the product \(pV\) is unchanged, as an isothermal change requires. The rise is not \(10\%\): restoring the product after the pressure has fallen to \(0.9\,p_{i}\) needs the volume multiplied by \(\dfrac{1}{0.9}\), not by \(1.1\).

\(\therefore\) the volume increases by about \(11\%\).

**(D)** \(W = Q\)

In a cyclic process the system is taken through a series of changes and is brought back to its initial state at the end of the cycle.

**Internal energy over a cycle.** The internal energy \(U\) is a state variable: it depends only on the state of the system and not on the path by which that state was reached. Since the initial and the final states of a cycle are the same state,

\(\Delta U = U_{\text{final}} - U_{\text{initial}} = 0\)

**Apply the first law.** The first law of thermodynamics is \(\Delta U = Q - W\), where \(Q\) is the heat supplied to the system and \(W\) is the work done by the system. Putting \(\Delta U = 0\),

\(0 = Q - W\)

\(\therefore W = Q\)

So in a cyclic process the whole of the heat supplied to the system appears as the work done by it. Note that \(Q\) and \(W\) are individually not zero — a cycle enclosing an area on the \(p\)-\(V\) diagram does a non-zero net work — it is only their difference that vanishes.

A system is said to be in **thermodynamic equilibrium** when the following three conditions of equilibrium are satisfied simultaneously.

**(a) Mechanical equilibrium.** A system is in mechanical equilibrium when there are no unbalanced forces within the system, and none between the system and its surroundings. Equivalently, the pressure throughout the system, and between the system and its surroundings, is the same and does not change with time. Any unbalanced force that does exist within the system gets neutralised with time, and the system then attains mechanical equilibrium.

**(b) Chemical equilibrium.** A system is in chemical equilibrium when there is no chemical reaction going on within the system, and no transfer of matter from one part of the system to another, such as diffusion or dissolution. The chemical composition of the system is therefore the same throughout and does not change with time.

**(c) Thermal equilibrium.** A system is in thermal equilibrium when the temperature is the same throughout the system, and the same as that of its surroundings, and does not change with time. Two systems in thermal contact are in thermal equilibrium when they do not transfer heat between each other.

Only when all three hold together can the system be described by a single set of state variables \(p\), \(V\) and \(T\).

**The system.** Consider a fixed mass of gas enclosed in a cylinder fitted at one end with a movable, massless and frictionless piston. The gas inside the cylinder is the system, and everything outside it is its environment. Let \(T_{S}\) be the temperature of the gas and \(T_{E}\) that of the environment.

**Internal energy.** The internal energy \(U\) of the gas is the total energy of all its molecules — the energy associated with their random, disordered motion. It is a microscopic quantity, and for an ideal gas it depends only on the temperature of the gas.

**Heating the system.** Bring the cylinder in contact with a source of heat, such as a burner, so that the source is at a higher temperature than the gas, \(T_{E} > T_{S}\). Heat is the energy that is transferred between a system and its environment because of a temperature difference between the two, so energy now flows from the burner into the gas. This heat \(Q\) taken in by the gas is positive.

The energy so received is shared among the gas molecules and increases the average kinetic energy of their random motion. The temperature of the gas therefore rises, and since the internal energy of the gas is the total energy of all its molecules, **the internal energy of the gas increases**.

**By how much.** By the first law of thermodynamics, \(\Delta U = Q - W\), where \(W\) is the work done by the gas. If the piston is clamped so that the volume of the gas stays constant, no work is done \((W = 0)\) and the whole of the heat supplied goes to raise the internal energy, \(\Delta U = Q\). If instead the piston is free to move, the gas expands and does work on the surroundings, so only the part \(Q - W\) of the heat supplied is left to raise the internal energy.

**The reverse case.** If the environment is at a lower temperature than the gas, \(T_{S} > T_{E}\), the flow is outward: \(Q\) is negative, the gas loses energy to its environment, its molecules slow down, and the internal energy of the gas decreases as it cools. If \(T_{S} = T_{E}\), the two are in thermal equilibrium, \(Q = 0\), and the internal energy does not change on this account.

**Data:** work done ON the gas \(= 104\) J; heat released by the gas \(= 125\) kJ. To find: \(\Delta U\).

**Sign convention.** The first law of thermodynamics is written \(\Delta U = Q - W\), where \(Q\) is the heat added TO the system and \(W\) is the work done BY the system. Both quantities here are given in the opposite sense, so both are negative.

The work is done on the gas, so

\(W = -104 \text{ J} = -0.104\) kJ

The heat is released by the gas, so

\(Q = -125\) kJ

**Change in internal energy.**

\(\Delta U = Q - W = (-125) - (-0.104)\)

\(\therefore \Delta U = -125 + 0.104 = -124.896\) kJ

**Check with the other form of the first law.** Writing it as \(\Delta U = Q + W_{\text{on}}\), where \(W_{\text{on}}\) is the work done on the system,

\(\Delta U = -125 + 0.104 = -124.896\) kJ, the same value. The sign does not depend on which of the two standard conventions is used.

**Reading the sign physically:** the gas gives out \(125\) kJ as heat and receives back only \(0.104\) kJ as work, so on balance nearly \(125\) kJ of energy leaves it and its internal energy must fall. The internal energy of the gas decreases by \(124.896\) kJ, that is by \(1.24896 \times 10^{5}\) J.

answer:
**The process.** An isothermal process is one in which the change in pressure and volume of a system takes place at a constant temperature, so \(\Delta T = 0\).

**Set up.** Consider one mole (in general \(n\) moles) of an ideal gas enclosed in a cylinder fitted with a movable, frictionless and massless piston, the walls of the cylinder being good conductors of heat so that the temperature \(T\) stays constant. Let the gas expand isothermally from an initial volume \(V_{i}\) to a final volume \(V_{f}\).

**Work in an infinitesimal change.** Let the pressure of the gas be \(p\) and let the piston move out so slowly that the gas is in equilibrium at every instant. If the volume increases by an infinitesimally small amount \(dV\), the work done by the gas is

\(dW = p\,dV\)

**Total work.** The total work done in taking the gas from \(V_{i}\) to \(V_{f}\) is obtained by integrating this over the whole change:

\(W = \displaystyle\int_{V_{i}}^{V_{f}} p\,dV\)

**Eliminate \(p\).** For \(n\) moles of an ideal gas, the equation of state is \(pV = nRT\), so

\(p = \dfrac{nRT}{V}\)

Substituting,

\(W = \displaystyle\int_{V_{i}}^{V_{f}} \dfrac{nRT}{V}\,dV\)

Since the process is isothermal, \(T\) is constant, and \(n\) and \(R\) are constants, so they can be taken outside the integral:

\(W = nRT \displaystyle\int_{V_{i}}^{V_{f}} \dfrac{dV}{V} = nRT\,\big[\ln V\big]_{V_{i}}^{V_{f}}\)

\(\therefore W = nRT \ln\left(\dfrac{V_{f}}{V_{i}}\right)\)

This is the required expression. Using \(\log_{10}\) it is written \(W = 2.303\,nRT \log_{10}\left(\dfrac{V_{f}}{V_{i}}\right)\).

**Heat exchanged.** The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on its temperature, so for an isothermal change \(\Delta U = 0\). The first law \(\Delta U = Q - W\) then gives

\(Q = W = nRT \ln\left(\dfrac{V_{f}}{V_{i}}\right)\)

so the whole of the heat supplied is converted into work.

**Check on the sign.** For an expansion \(V_{f} > V_{i}\), the logarithm is positive and \(W\) is positive — the gas does work on its surroundings, as it must while pushing the piston out. For a compression \(V_{f} < V_{i}\), the logarithm is negative and \(W\) is negative — work is done on the gas.

**Isothermal process.** A process in which the change in the pressure and the volume of a system takes place at a **constant temperature** is called an isothermal process. For such a change \(\Delta T = 0\). It is possible only when the system is in good thermal contact with its surroundings and the change is carried out extremely slowly, so that thermal equilibrium is maintained throughout. Since the temperature is constant, Boyle's law holds and the equation of state of an ideal gas is \(pV = \) constant, i.e. \(p_{i}V_{i} = p_{f}V_{f}\). The \(p\)-\(V\) curve of such a change is called an isotherm. Melting of ice and boiling of water are examples.

**Work done by the gas.** Consider \(n\) moles of an ideal gas in a cylinder fitted with a movable, frictionless and massless piston, held at a constant temperature \(T\). Let the gas expand from an initial volume \(V_{i}\) to a final volume \(V_{f}\).

If the gas at pressure \(p\) expands by an infinitesimally small volume \(dV\), the work done by it is

\(dW = p\,dV\)

The total work done in the whole expansion is therefore

\(W = \displaystyle\int_{V_{i}}^{V_{f}} p\,dV\)

For an ideal gas \(pV = nRT\), so \(p = \dfrac{nRT}{V}\). Substituting,

\(W = \displaystyle\int_{V_{i}}^{V_{f}} \dfrac{nRT}{V}\,dV\)

The process is isothermal, so \(T\) is constant and \(nRT\) can be taken out of the integral:

\(W = nRT \displaystyle\int_{V_{i}}^{V_{f}} \dfrac{dV}{V} = nRT\,\big[\ln V\big]_{V_{i}}^{V_{f}}\)

\(\therefore W = nRT \ln\left(\dfrac{V_{f}}{V_{i}}\right) = 2.303\,nRT \log_{10}\left(\dfrac{V_{f}}{V_{i}}\right)\)

**Heat supplied.** The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on its temperature, so \(\Delta U = 0\) for an isothermal change, and the first law \(\Delta U = Q - W\) reduces to

\(Q = W = nRT \ln\left(\dfrac{V_{f}}{V_{i}}\right)\)

All the heat taken in by the gas is thus spent in doing work.

**Check on the sign.** In an expansion \(V_{f} > V_{i}\), so \(\ln(V_{f}/V_{i}) > 0\) and \(W\) is positive — the gas does work on its surroundings while pushing the piston out. In a compression \(V_{f} < V_{i}\) and \(W\) comes out negative, meaning work is done on the gas.

**Data:** \(p = 2 \times 10^{5}\) N/m\(^{2}\) (constant), \(V_{i} = 6 \times 10^{-3}\) m\(^{3}\), work done in compressing the gas \(= 150\) J. To find: \(V_{f}\).

**Relation.** For a change at constant pressure the work done BY the gas is

\(W = \displaystyle\int_{V_{i}}^{V_{f}} p\,dV = p\,(V_{f} - V_{i})\)

**Sign of the work.** The gas is **compressed**, so the work is done on the gas and the work done by the gas is negative:

\(W = -150\) J

**Change in volume.**

\(V_{f} - V_{i} = \dfrac{W}{p} = \dfrac{-150}{2 \times 10^{5}} = -7.5 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^{3}\)

The negative sign confirms that the volume decreases, as it must in a compression.

**Final volume.**

\(V_{f} = V_{i} + (V_{f} - V_{i}) = 6 \times 10^{-3} - 7.5 \times 10^{-4}\)

\(= 60 \times 10^{-4} - 7.5 \times 10^{-4}\)

\(\therefore V_{f} = 52.5 \times 10^{-4} = 5.25 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^{3}\)

**Check.** Substituting back, \(p\,(V_{f} - V_{i}) = 2 \times 10^{5} \times (5.25 \times 10^{-3} - 6 \times 10^{-3}) = 2 \times 10^{5} \times (-7.5 \times 10^{-4}) = -150\) J, whose magnitude is the given \(150\) J. The final volume is \(5.25\) litre against an initial \(6\) litre, a compression of a little over one-tenth, which is consistent with the modest work of \(150\) J done at this pressure.
twin: A gas enclosed in a cylinder is expanded to double its initial volume at a constant pressure of one atmosphere. How much work is done in this process?.

answer:
**Data:** the gas is ideal and mono-atomic, so \(\gamma = \dfrac{C_{p}}{C_{v}} = \dfrac{5}{3}\); the compression is adiabatic; \(T_{f} = 2T_{i}\). To find: \(\dfrac{p_{f}}{p_{i}}\).

**Relation.** For a reversible adiabatic change of an ideal gas,

\(pV^{\gamma} = \) constant

Using the equation of state \(pV = nRT\) to eliminate \(V\), i.e. putting \(V = \dfrac{nRT}{p}\),

\(p\left(\dfrac{nRT}{p}\right)^{\gamma} = \) constant, so \(T^{\gamma}p^{1-\gamma} = \) constant

Hence for the initial and the final states,

\(T_{i}^{\gamma}\,p_{i}^{1-\gamma} = T_{f}^{\gamma}\,p_{f}^{1-\gamma}\), i.e. \(\dfrac{p_{f}}{p_{i}} = \left(\dfrac{T_{f}}{T_{i}}\right)^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma - 1}}\)

**Evaluate the exponent.**

\(\gamma - 1 = \dfrac{5}{3} - 1 = \dfrac{2}{3}\), so \(\dfrac{\gamma}{\gamma - 1} = \dfrac{5/3}{2/3} = \dfrac{5}{2} = 2.5\)

**Substitute.**

\(\dfrac{p_{f}}{p_{i}} = (2)^{5/2} = 4\sqrt{2}\)

\(\therefore \dfrac{p_{f}}{p_{i}} = 5.657\), i.e. \(p_{f} : p_{i} = 4\sqrt{2} : 1\)

**Independent check through the volume.** From \(TV^{\gamma - 1} = \) constant,

\(\dfrac{V_{f}}{V_{i}} = \left(\dfrac{T_{i}}{T_{f}}\right)^{\frac{1}{\gamma - 1}} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{3/2} = 0.3536\)

and then from \(pV^{\gamma} = \) constant,

\(\dfrac{p_{f}}{p_{i}} = \left(\dfrac{V_{i}}{V_{f}}\right)^{\gamma} = (2.828)^{5/3} = 5.657\), which agrees.

The ratio is greater than \(1\), as it must be: the gas is compressed and its temperature rises, so its pressure has to rise as well.
twin: An ideal monatomic gas is adiabatically compressed so that its final temperature is twice its initial temperature. What is the ratio of the final pressure to its initial pressure?

answer:
**Data:** \(n = 0.5\) mol, \(T = 300\) K, \(V_{i} = 2.0\) litre, \(V_{f} = 6.0\) litre, the expansion is isothermal. Take \(R = 8.314\) J mol\(^{-1}\) K\(^{-1}\). To find: the work done by the gas.

**Relation.** In an isothermal change the pressure of an ideal gas is \(p = \dfrac{nRT}{V}\), so the work done by the gas is

\(W = \displaystyle\int_{V_{i}}^{V_{f}} p\,dV = nRT \displaystyle\int_{V_{i}}^{V_{f}} \dfrac{dV}{V} = nRT \ln\left(\dfrac{V_{f}}{V_{i}}\right)\)

**Substitute.** The volumes appear only as a ratio, so they need not be converted to m\(^{3}\):

\(\dfrac{V_{f}}{V_{i}} = \dfrac{6.0}{2.0} = 3\), and \(\ln 3 = 1.0986\)

\(W = 0.5 \times 8.314 \times 300 \times 1.0986\)

\(= 1247.1 \times 1.0986\)

\(\therefore W = 1370\ \text{J} = 1.37\ \text{kJ}\)

**Check.** The work is positive, as it must be for an expansion — the gas pushes the piston out and does work on its surroundings. As a rough bound, the gas does at least \(nRT\left(1 - \dfrac{V_{i}}{V_{f}}\right) = 1247.1 \times \dfrac{2}{3} = 831\) J (the work at the lower, final pressure) and at most \(nRT\left(\dfrac{V_{f}}{V_{i}} - 1\right) = 1247.1 \times 2 = 2494\) J (the work at the higher, initial pressure); \(1370\) J lies between the two, so the value is consistent.

Since the internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on its temperature, \(\Delta U = 0\) here, and by the first law the heat supplied to the gas is \(Q = W = 1.37\) kJ.
twin: 0.5 mole of gas at temp 300 K expands isothermally from an initial volume of 2.0L to final volume of 6.0L. (a) What is the work done by the gas ? (\(R = 8.319\) J mol\(^{-1}\) K\(^{-1}\)), (b) How much heat is supplied to the gas?
